text: Background activity
An EEG activity representing the setting in which a given normal or abnormal pattern appears and from which such pattern is distinguished.
EEG activity that provides the setting in which a normal or abnormal pattern occurs and from which that pattern is differentiated.
The EEG activity within which a given normal or abnormal pattern appears and against which it is distinguished.
A normal or abnormal pattern emerges within this EEG activity and is distinguished from it.
This EEG activity forms the context for the appearance of a particular normal or abnormal pattern, which is differentiated from that activity.
The setting for a given normal or abnormal pattern is provided by EEG activity from which the pattern is distinguished.
EEG activity serves as the context in which a particular normal or abnormal pattern appears and is recognized as distinct.
A given normal or abnormal pattern appears against this EEG activity, which constitutes its setting and from which it is distinguished.
Episodes
Clinical episodes or electrographic seizures
These are clinical episodes or electrographic seizures.
The events consist of clinical episodes or electrographic seizures.
Either clinical episodes or electrographic seizures are described.
The description encompasses clinical episodes or electrographic seizures.
The events are either clinical episodes or electrographic seizures.
Clinical episodes or electrographic seizures constitute these events.
This refers to clinical episodes or electrographic seizures.
Modulators

External stimuli / interventions or changes in the alertness level (sleep) that modify: the background activity, or how often a graphoelement is occurring, or change other features of the graphoelement (like intra-burst frequency). Examples of modulators are: hyperventilation, intermittent photic stimulation, administration of a medication during the recording.

External stimuli or interventions, or changes in alertness level (sleep), alter background activity, the frequency of a graphoelement's occurrence, or other graphoelement features such as intra-burst frequency. Modulators include hyperventilation, intermittent photic stimulation, and medication administration during recording.

Modulators are external stimuli, interventions, or alertness-level changes (sleep) that change background activity, how often a graphoelement occurs, or its other features, including intra-burst frequency. Examples are hyperventilation, intermittent photic stimulation, and administering medication during the recording.

Background activity, graphoelement occurrence frequency, or other features of a graphoelement, such as intra-burst frequency, may be modified by external stimuli or interventions or by changes in alertness level (sleep). Examples of these modulators include hyperventilation, intermittent photic stimulation, and administration of medication during recording.

Changes to background activity, to how often a graphoelement appears, or to other graphoelement characteristics (for example, intra-burst frequency) result from external stimuli, interventions, or changes in alertness level (sleep). Hyperventilation, intermittent photic stimulation, and medication given during recording are examples of modulators.

External stimuli and interventions, together with changes in alertness level (sleep), serve as modulators when they modify background activity, graphoelement occurrence frequency, or other features such as intra-burst frequency. Examples include hyperventilation, intermittent photic stimulation, and medication administration during the recording.

A modulator changes background activity, the rate at which a graphoelement occurs, or another graphoelement feature such as intra-burst frequency, through external stimulation, intervention, or an alertness-level change (sleep). Hyperventilation, intermittent photic stimulation, and administration of medication during recording exemplify modulators.

Hyperventilation, intermittent photic stimulation, and medication administration during recording are examples of external stimuli or interventions that act as modulators. External stimuli or interventions, or changes in alertness level (sleep), modify background activity, how frequently a graphoelement occurs, or other features of that graphoelement, such as intra-burst frequency.
Interictal findings

EEG patterns / transients that are distinguished form the background activity, considered abnormal, but are not recorded during ictal period (seizure) or postictal period; the presence of interictal findings does not necessarily imply that the patient has epilepsy.

Abnormal EEG patterns or transients distinguishable from background activity are recorded outside the ictal (seizure) and postictal periods; interictal findings do not necessarily mean that the patient has epilepsy.

These EEG patterns or transients are considered abnormal and stand apart from background activity, but are not recorded during the ictal (seizure) or postictal period. Their interictal presence does not necessarily imply epilepsy in the patient.

EEG patterns or transients that differ from background activity and are judged abnormal occur in recordings outside the ictal (seizure) and postictal periods. Interictal findings alone do not necessarily imply that the patient has epilepsy.

The findings are abnormal EEG patterns or transients distinguishable from the background, recorded neither during the ictal period (seizure) nor during the postictal period. The patient does not necessarily have epilepsy simply because interictal findings are present.

Considered abnormal, these EEG patterns or transients are differentiated from background activity and are not recorded in the ictal (seizure) or postictal period; the presence of interictal findings does not necessarily indicate that the patient has epilepsy.

Outside the ictal period (seizure) and the postictal period, EEG patterns or transients may be distinguished from background activity and considered abnormal. Such interictal findings do not necessarily imply epilepsy in the patient.

These are EEG patterns or transients judged abnormal and distinct from background activity, with recording outside both the ictal (seizure) and postictal periods. A patient's epilepsy is not necessarily implied by the presence of interictal findings.
Patterns of uncertain significance

EEG graphoelements or rhythms that resemble abnormal patterns but that are not necessarily associated with a pathology, and the physician does not consider them abnormal in the context of the scored recording (like normal variants and patterns).

EEG graphoelements or rhythms resemble abnormal patterns without necessarily being associated with pathology; in the scored recording, the physician does not judge them abnormal, as with normal variants and patterns.

These EEG graphoelements or rhythms look like abnormal patterns, but need not be associated with pathology and are not considered abnormal by the physician in the context of the scored recording, for example normal variants and patterns.

In the scored recording, the physician regards these EEG graphoelements or rhythms as not abnormal, despite their resemblance to abnormal patterns and their not necessarily being associated with pathology. Normal variants and patterns are examples.

Resembling abnormal patterns, these EEG graphoelements or rhythms are not necessarily linked to pathology and are not judged abnormal by the physician within the scored recording, as illustrated by normal variants and patterns.

Normal variants and patterns exemplify EEG graphoelements or rhythms that mimic abnormal patterns but are not necessarily associated with pathology and that the physician does not consider abnormal in the scored recording.

The EEG graphoelements or rhythms have an appearance resembling abnormal patterns, yet an association with pathology is not necessary, and the physician does not classify them as abnormal in the context of the scored recording, as with normal variants and patterns.

The physician does not consider these EEG graphoelements or rhythms abnormal for the scored recording, although they resemble abnormal patterns; they are not necessarily associated with pathology, with normal variants and patterns as examples.
Physiologic patterns
EEG graphoelements or rhythms that are considered normal. They only should be scored if the physician considers that they have a specific clinical significance for the recording.
EEG graphoelements or rhythms regarded as normal should be scored only when the physician considers them to have specific clinical significance for the recording.
These are normal EEG graphoelements or rhythms, to be scored only if the physician judges that they carry a specific clinical significance for the recording.
Only a physician's assessment of specific clinical significance for the recording warrants scoring these EEG graphoelements or rhythms, which are considered normal.
Scoring of EEG graphoelements or rhythms considered normal is appropriate only if the physician regards them as specifically clinically significant for the recording.
The physician should score these normal EEG graphoelements or rhythms only when they are considered to have particular clinical significance for that recording.
EEG graphoelements or rhythms are considered normal here; they should receive a score only when the physician assigns them specific clinical significance in the recording.

If the physician considers these EEG graphoelements or rhythms specifically clinically significant for the recording, they should be scored; otherwise, these elements or rhythms considered normal should not be scored.
Sleep and drowsiness

The features of the “ongoing” activity during sleep are scored here. If abnormal graphoelements appear, disappear or change their morphology during sleep, that is not scored here but at the entry corresponding to that graphooelement (as a modulator).

Features of ongoing activity during sleep are scored here. The appearance, disappearance, or morphological change of abnormal graphoelements during sleep is instead scored as a modulator in the corresponding graphoelement entry.

This entry scores the characteristics of ongoing sleep activity. If abnormal graphoelements emerge, vanish, or change morphology during sleep, those changes are scored under the relevant graphoelement as a modulator, rather than here.

Score ongoing activity features during sleep in this entry, but record abnormal graphoelements appearing, disappearing, or changing morphology during sleep as modulators in their respective graphoelement entries.

The ongoing activity's features during sleep belong here for scoring; sleep-related appearance, disappearance, or morphological changes of abnormal graphoelements belong in the entry for that graphoelement, as a modulator.

Here, scoring concerns the features of ongoing activity in sleep. Abnormal graphoelements that appear, disappear, or alter their morphology during sleep are scored as a modulator at the corresponding graphoelement entry instead.

Use this entry to score features of ongoing activity during sleep. Use the corresponding graphoelement entry, as a modulator, for abnormal graphoelements appearing, disappearing, or changing morphology during sleep.

Ongoing sleep activity is scored here for its features, whereas the appearance, disappearance, or change in morphology of abnormal graphoelements during sleep is scored as a modulator under the appropriate graphoelement.
Alpha activity
EEG rhythm in the alpha range (8-13 Hz) which is considered part of the background (ongoing) activity but does not fulfil the criteria of the posterior dominant rhythm (alpha rhythm).
An EEG rhythm in the alpha range (8-13 Hz) is regarded as background (ongoing) activity but does not meet the criteria for the posterior dominant rhythm (alpha rhythm).
This alpha-range EEG rhythm (8-13 Hz) forms part of the background (ongoing) activity without satisfying the posterior dominant rhythm (alpha rhythm) criteria.
Background (ongoing) activity includes this EEG rhythm at 8-13 Hz in the alpha range, although it fails to fulfil the criteria for the posterior dominant rhythm (alpha rhythm).
The EEG rhythm falls within the alpha range, 8-13 Hz, and is considered background (ongoing) activity, while not qualifying as the posterior dominant rhythm (alpha rhythm).
An EEG rhythm at 8-13 Hz belongs to the alpha range and is considered part of ongoing background activity, but the criteria for the posterior dominant rhythm (alpha rhythm) are not met.
Although regarded as part of background (ongoing) activity, this EEG rhythm in the 8-13 Hz alpha range does not fulfil posterior dominant rhythm (alpha rhythm) criteria.
The posterior dominant rhythm (alpha rhythm) criteria are not satisfied by this alpha-range (8-13 Hz) EEG rhythm, which is considered part of background (ongoing) activity.
Amplitude asymmetry
A difference in amplitude between the homologous area on opposite sides of the head that consistently exceeds 50%.
The amplitude difference between homologous areas on opposite sides of the head consistently exceeds 50%.
Homologous regions on opposite sides of the head show a consistently greater than 50% difference in amplitude.
A persistent amplitude difference of more than 50% exists between corresponding areas on the two sides of the head.
Amplitudes in homologous areas on opposite sides of the head consistently differ by over 50%.
Comparing homologous areas on opposite sides of the head reveals an amplitude difference that is consistently above 50%.
There is a consistently greater than 50% amplitude difference across homologous areas on opposing sides of the head.
An amplitude difference exceeding 50% is consistently present between homologous areas on the head's opposite sides.
Beta activity

EEG rhythm between 14 and 40 Hz, which is considered part of the background (ongoing) activity but does not fulfil the criteria of the posterior dominant rhythm. Most characteristically: a rhythm from 14 to 40 Hz recorded over the fronto-central regions of the head during wakefulness. Amplitude of the beta rhythm varies but is mostly below 30 µV. Other beta rhythms are most prominent in other locations or are diffuse.

An EEG rhythm at 14-40 Hz is considered background (ongoing) activity but does not meet posterior dominant rhythm criteria. Characteristically, it is recorded over fronto-central head regions during wakefulness. Beta rhythm amplitude varies but is mostly below 30 µV; other beta rhythms predominate elsewhere or are diffuse.

The 14-40 Hz EEG rhythm forms part of background (ongoing) activity without fulfilling the posterior dominant rhythm criteria. Its most characteristic presentation is a 14-40 Hz rhythm over fronto-central regions of the head in wakefulness. Beta amplitude is variable, usually below 30 µV, while other beta rhythms are most prominent at other locations or diffusely distributed.

Considered ongoing background activity, this EEG rhythm between 14 and 40 Hz does not qualify as the posterior dominant rhythm. It is most characteristically a 14-40 Hz rhythm recorded over fronto-central head regions during wakefulness. The beta rhythm has variable amplitude, mostly under 30 µV; other beta rhythms are diffuse or maximal elsewhere.

This EEG rhythm belongs to background (ongoing) activity at 14-40 Hz but fails to satisfy posterior dominant rhythm criteria. A 14-40 Hz rhythm over the fronto-central head regions during wakefulness is most characteristic. Its beta amplitude varies and is mostly less than 30 µV. Other beta rhythms are prominent in different locations or are diffuse.

A 14-40 Hz EEG rhythm that is regarded as background (ongoing) activity does not fulfil the criteria of the posterior dominant rhythm. Most characteristically it occurs at 14-40 Hz over fronto-central regions during wakefulness. Beta rhythm amplitude, though variable, is predominantly below 30 µV, and other beta rhythms predominate at other sites or are diffuse.

The EEG rhythm is considered part of ongoing background activity, spans 14-40 Hz, and does not meet the posterior dominant rhythm criteria. It is characteristically recorded at 14-40 Hz over the fronto-central head regions during wakefulness. Variable beta amplitude is mostly below 30 µV; other beta rhythms show prominence elsewhere or a diffuse distribution.

Most characteristically, a rhythm of 14-40 Hz is recorded over fronto-central head regions in wakefulness. This 14-40 Hz EEG rhythm is considered background (ongoing) activity but does not satisfy posterior dominant rhythm criteria. Beta amplitude varies, mostly remaining below 30 µV, while other beta rhythms are diffuse or most prominent in other locations.
Delta activity
EEG rhythm in the delta (under 4 Hz) range that does not belong to the posterior dominant rhythm (scored under other organised rhythms).
An EEG rhythm in the delta range (under 4 Hz) is outside the posterior dominant rhythm and is scored under other organised rhythms.
This delta-range EEG rhythm, below 4 Hz, does not belong to the posterior dominant rhythm; score it under other organised rhythms.
Scored among other organised rhythms, the EEG rhythm is in the delta range under 4 Hz and is not part of the posterior dominant rhythm.
The EEG rhythm occurs below 4 Hz in the delta range, does not form part of the posterior dominant rhythm, and is scored under other organised rhythms.
A delta EEG rhythm under 4 Hz that is not included in the posterior dominant rhythm is scored under other organised rhythms.
Other organised rhythms is the scoring entry for this EEG rhythm in the delta range (under 4 Hz), which is separate from the posterior dominant rhythm.
Outside the posterior dominant rhythm, this EEG rhythm lies in the delta range below 4 Hz and belongs under other organised rhythms for scoring.
Electrocerebral inactivity
Absence of any ongoing cortical electric activities; in all leads EEG is isoelectric or only contains artefacts. Sensitivity has to be increased up to 2 µV/mm; recording time: at least 30 minutes.
No ongoing cortical electrical activity is present; EEG in every lead is isoelectric or contains only artefacts. Sensitivity must be increased to 2 µV/mm, and recording must last at least 30 minutes.
Ongoing cortical electrical activity is absent, with all EEG leads showing an isoelectric trace or artefacts alone. Increase sensitivity up to 2 µV/mm and record for at least 30 minutes.

Every EEG lead is isoelectric or contains only artefacts, indicating absence of ongoing cortical electrical activity. Sensitivity has to be increased to 2 µV/mm; the recording duration is at least 30 minutes.

There is no ongoing cortical electrical activity, and the EEG is isoelectric or limited to artefacts in all leads. The required sensitivity increase is to 2 µV/mm, with a minimum recording time of 30 minutes.

Absence of ongoing cortical electrical activity is accompanied by isoelectric EEG or artefacts only across all leads. Recording must continue for 30 minutes or longer, with sensitivity increased to 2 µV/mm.

An isoelectric EEG or an EEG containing only artefacts in every lead accompanies the absence of any ongoing cortical electrical activity. Raise sensitivity to 2 µV/mm and ensure at least 30 minutes of recording.

With ongoing cortical electrical activity absent, all EEG leads are isoelectric or show artefacts alone; sensitivity must be increased up to 2 µV/mm and the recording must be at least 30 minutes long.
Generalised suppression burst
EEG pattern consisting of bursts (activity appearing and disappearing abruptly) interrupted by periods of low amplitude (below 20 µV) and which occurs simultaneously over all head regions.
An EEG pattern occurring simultaneously across all head regions comprises bursts, with abrupt appearance and disappearance of activity, separated by low-amplitude periods below 20 µV.
Bursts of abruptly appearing and disappearing activity are interrupted by periods under 20 µV in an EEG pattern simultaneous over all head regions.
The EEG pattern consists of abrupt-onset, abrupt-offset bursts interspersed with low-amplitude periods below 20 µV, occurring at the same time throughout all regions of the head.
Across all head regions simultaneously, the EEG shows bursts of activity that appear and disappear abruptly, interrupted by low-amplitude intervals under 20 µV.
Activity appears and disappears abruptly in bursts, with intervening periods of amplitude below 20 µV, forming an EEG pattern simultaneous over all head regions.
Low-amplitude periods below 20 µV interrupt bursts of abruptly appearing and disappearing activity in this EEG pattern, which occurs simultaneously across all head regions.
This EEG pattern is simultaneous throughout the head and alternates bursts of activity appearing and disappearing abruptly with interrupting low-amplitude periods below 20 µV.
Mu rhythm

EEG rhythm at 7-11 Hz composed of arch-shaped waves occurring over the central or centro-parietal regions of the scalp during wakefulness. Amplitudes varies but is mostly below 50 µV. Blocked or attenuated most clearly by contralateral movement, thought of movement, readiness to move or tactile stimulation.

An EEG rhythm of arch-shaped waves at 7-11 Hz occurs over central or centro-parietal scalp regions during wakefulness. Amplitude varies but is mostly below 50 µV. Contralateral movement, thought of movement, readiness to move, or tactile stimulation most clearly blocks or attenuates it.

During wakefulness, arch-shaped waves form a 7-11 Hz EEG rhythm over central or centro-parietal scalp regions. Its variable amplitude is mostly under 50 µV, and blocking or attenuation is clearest with contralateral movement, thinking of movement, readiness to move, or tactile stimulation.

The 7-11 Hz EEG rhythm comprises arch-shaped waves in central or centro-parietal scalp regions in wakefulness. Amplitudes are variable, mainly below 50 µV; contralateral movement, thought of movement, readiness to move, and tactile stimulation most clearly block or attenuate the rhythm.

Over central or centro-parietal scalp regions in wakefulness, this EEG rhythm consists of arch-shaped waves at 7-11 Hz. Though variable, its amplitude is mostly below 50 µV. It is most clearly blocked or attenuated by contralateral movement, thought of movement, readiness to move, or tactile stimulation.

Arch-shaped waves at 7-11 Hz make up an EEG rhythm seen over central or centro-parietal scalp regions while awake. Amplitude varies, usually remaining below 50 µV, and the clearest blocking or attenuation occurs with contralateral movement, thought of movement, readiness to move, or tactile stimulation.

This EEG rhythm occurs in wakefulness at 7-11 Hz over the central or centro-parietal scalp and has arch-shaped waves. Its amplitude is variable but mostly less than 50 µV. Contralateral movement, thinking about movement, being ready to move, or tactile stimulation provides the clearest blocking or attenuation.

Contralateral movement, thought of movement, readiness to move, or tactile stimulation most clearly blocks or attenuates this EEG rhythm. It consists of arch-shaped 7-11 Hz waves over central or centro-parietal scalp regions during wakefulness, with variable amplitude mostly below 50 µV.

Posterior dominant rhythm

Rhythmic activity occurring during wakefulness over the posterior regions of the head, generally with maximum amplitudes over the occipital areas. Amplitude varies. Best seen with eyes closed and during physical relaxation and relative mental inactivity. Blocked or attenuated by attention, especially visual, and mental effort. In adults this is the alpha rhythm, and the frequency is 8 – 13 Hz. However the frequency can be higher or lower than this range (often a supra or sub-harmonic of alpha frequency) and is called alpha variant rhythm (fast and slow alpha variant rhythm). In children, the normal range of the frequency of the posterior dominant rhythm is age-dependant.

Rhythmic activity during wakefulness occurs over posterior head regions, generally with greatest amplitude occipitally, and has variable amplitude. It is best seen with closed eyes, physical relaxation, and relative mental inactivity, and is blocked or attenuated by attention, especially visual attention, and mental effort. In adults it is the alpha rhythm at 8-13 Hz, but a higher or lower frequency, often a supra- or sub-harmonic of alpha frequency, is called a fast or slow alpha variant rhythm. In children, the normal posterior dominant rhythm frequency range depends on age.

This variable-amplitude rhythm is present over posterior head regions in wakefulness, usually maximal over occipital areas. Closed eyes with physical relaxation and relative mental inactivity show it best; attention, particularly visual, and mental effort block or attenuate it. Adults have the 8-13 Hz alpha rhythm, though frequencies above or below this range, often supra- or sub-harmonics of alpha frequency, are termed fast and slow alpha variant rhythms. The normal frequency range of the posterior dominant rhythm in children is age-dependent.

During wakefulness, posterior rhythmic activity has variable amplitude that is generally highest in occipital areas. It is clearest with eyes closed during physical relaxation and relative mental inactivity and is blocked or attenuated by attention, especially visual, and mental effort. In adults, the activity is the alpha rhythm, with a frequency of 8-13 Hz. Higher or lower frequencies, often supra- or sub-harmonics of alpha frequency, constitute fast or slow alpha variant rhythms. Children's normal posterior dominant rhythm frequency range varies with age.

The rhythmic activity occurs posteriorly during wakefulness, usually reaching maximum amplitude over occipital areas; amplitude varies. Eyes closed, physical relaxation, and relative mental inactivity provide the best conditions for seeing it. Attention, especially visual attention, and mental effort block or attenuate it. The adult rhythm is alpha at 8-13 Hz; a frequency above or below that range, often a supra- or sub-harmonic of alpha frequency, is called an alpha variant rhythm, fast or slow. The normal posterior dominant rhythm frequency range is age-dependent in children.

Posterior head regions show rhythmic activity in wakefulness, with variable amplitude generally maximal occipitally. It is best observed during physical relaxation and relative mental inactivity with eyes closed, while attention, particularly visual, and mental effort block or attenuate it. The adult alpha rhythm is 8-13 Hz, although higher or lower frequencies, often supra- or sub-harmonics of alpha frequency, are called fast or slow alpha variant rhythms. In children, age determines the normal range of posterior dominant rhythm frequency.

With amplitude varying and generally greatest over occipital areas, this rhythm occurs over posterior head regions while awake. It is most evident with eyes closed and during physical relaxation and relative mental inactivity; attention, especially visual, and mental effort block or attenuate it. It is the alpha rhythm in adults, at 8-13 Hz, but frequencies higher or lower than that range, often supra- or sub-harmonics of alpha frequency, are termed fast or slow alpha variant rhythms. In children, the normal posterior dominant rhythm frequency range is dependent on age.

Attention, especially visual attention, and mental effort block or attenuate posterior rhythmic activity seen in wakefulness. Its variable amplitude is usually maximal over occipital areas, and it is best seen with closed eyes, physical relaxation, and relative mental inactivity. In adults it is the 8-13 Hz alpha rhythm; frequencies outside that range, higher or lower and often supra- or sub-harmonics of alpha frequency, are called fast or slow alpha variant rhythms. Children's normal posterior dominant rhythm frequency range depends on age.
Reactivity
Susceptibility of individual rhythms or the EEG as a whole to change following sensory stimulation or other physiologic actions. (The type of stimulus has to be specified in free-text).
Individual rhythms or the entire EEG are susceptible to change after sensory stimulation or other physiologic actions; specify the stimulus type in free text.
This describes the capacity of individual rhythms or the EEG as a whole to change following sensory stimulation or other physiologic actions. The type of stimulus must be stated in free text.
Sensory stimulation or other physiologic actions can change individual rhythms or the whole EEG; the stimulus type has to be specified in free text.
The susceptibility of the whole EEG or individual rhythms to change in response to sensory stimulation or other physiologic actions is described, with the stimulus type specified in free text.
Following sensory stimulation or other physiologic actions, individual rhythms or the EEG as a whole may change. State the type of stimulus in free text.
A change after sensory stimulation or another physiologic action can occur in individual rhythms or in the EEG as a whole; free text must identify the stimulus type.
Specify the stimulus type in free text when describing the susceptibility of individual rhythms or the entire EEG to change following sensory stimulation or other physiologic actions.
Reactivity to eye opening /closure
Change (disappearance or measurable decrease in amplitude) of a posterior dominant rhythm following eye-opening. Eye closure has the opposite effect.
Eye opening causes the posterior dominant rhythm to disappear or measurably decrease in amplitude; eye closure has the opposite effect.
The posterior dominant rhythm changes after eye opening through disappearance or a measurable amplitude decrease, with the reverse effect on eye closure.
Following eye opening, the posterior dominant rhythm disappears or shows a measurable decrease in amplitude, while closing the eyes produces the opposite effect.
A disappearance or measurable amplitude reduction of the posterior dominant rhythm follows eye opening; closing the eyes has the reverse effect.
Opening the eyes is followed by loss of the posterior dominant rhythm or a measurable fall in its amplitude. Eye closure acts in the opposite way.
The change in posterior dominant rhythm after opening the eyes is disappearance or measurable amplitude decrease, whereas eye closure has the opposing effect.
The posterior dominant rhythm responds to eye opening by disappearing or decreasing measurably in amplitude, and to eye closure with the opposite effect.
Suppression (of background activity)
Periods showing activity under 10 µV (referential montage) and interrupting the background (ongoing) activity.
Periods of activity below 10 µV in a referential montage interrupt the background (ongoing) activity.
Background (ongoing) activity is interrupted by periods showing activity under 10 µV on a referential montage.
These are interruptions of ongoing background activity comprising periods below 10 µV in a referential montage.
On a referential montage, activity remains under 10 µV during periods that interrupt background (ongoing) activity.
The background (ongoing) activity contains interrupting periods with activity of less than 10 µV in a referential montage.
Activity below 10 µV, as seen with a referential montage, occurs in periods interrupting ongoing background activity.
Interruptions of background (ongoing) activity show activity under 10 µV when recorded in a referential montage.
Theta activity
EEG rhythm in the theta (4-8 Hz) range that does not belong to the posterior dominant rhythm (scored under other organised rhythms).
An EEG rhythm in the theta range (4-8 Hz) is not part of the posterior dominant rhythm and is scored under other organised rhythms.
This 4-8 Hz theta-range EEG rhythm does not belong to the posterior dominant rhythm; it is scored among other organised rhythms.
Other organised rhythms is the scoring category for this EEG rhythm in the theta range, 4-8 Hz, outside the posterior dominant rhythm.
The EEG rhythm lies in the theta range at 4-8 Hz, is separate from the posterior dominant rhythm, and is scored under other organised rhythms.
Scored under other organised rhythms, this EEG rhythm at 4-8 Hz falls within the theta range and does not belong to the posterior dominant rhythm.
An EEG rhythm of 4-8 Hz in the theta range that is outside the posterior dominant rhythm belongs under other organised rhythms for scoring.
The posterior dominant rhythm does not include this theta-range (4-8 Hz) EEG rhythm, which is scored under other organised rhythms.

K complex

A burst of somewhat variable appearance, consisting most commonly of a high voltage negative slow wave followed by a smaller positive slow wave frequently associated with a sleep spindle. Duration > 0.5 s. Amplitude is generally maximal in the frontal vertex. K complexes occur during non- REM sleep, apparently spontaneously, or in response to sudden sensory / auditory stimuli, and are not specific for any individual sensory modality.

A burst of somewhat variable appearance most often comprises a high-voltage negative slow wave followed by a smaller positive slow wave, frequently associated with a sleep spindle. Duration exceeds 0.5 s, and amplitude is generally greatest at the frontal vertex. K complexes occur during non-REM sleep, apparently spontaneously or after sudden sensory or auditory stimuli, without specificity to any individual sensory modality.

K complexes are somewhat variable bursts, most commonly a high-voltage negative slow wave followed by a smaller positive slow wave and frequently associated with a sleep spindle. They last >0.5 s and generally reach maximum amplitude at the frontal vertex. During non-REM sleep they appear apparently spontaneously or in response to sudden sensory or auditory stimuli and are not specific to a particular sensory modality.

The burst varies somewhat in appearance but usually consists of a high-voltage negative slow wave followed by a smaller positive slow wave, often associated with a sleep spindle. Its duration is >0.5 s and its amplitude generally maximal at the frontal vertex. K complexes arise in non-REM sleep, apparently spontaneously or in response to sudden sensory or auditory stimuli, with no specificity for any individual sensory modality.

During non-REM sleep, K complexes occur apparently spontaneously or after sudden sensory or auditory stimulation; they are not specific to an individual sensory modality. These somewhat variable bursts most commonly contain a high-voltage negative slow wave followed by a smaller positive slow wave, frequently associated with a sleep spindle. They last longer than 0.5 s and are generally largest at the frontal vertex.

A somewhat variable burst, lasting more than 0.5 s and generally maximal in amplitude at the frontal vertex, most commonly consists of a high-voltage negative slow wave followed by a smaller positive slow wave, frequently associated with a sleep spindle. K complexes occur in non-REM sleep, apparently spontaneously or following sudden sensory or auditory stimuli, and do not correspond specifically to any single sensory modality.

Most commonly, a high-voltage negative slow wave and a subsequent smaller positive slow wave form the somewhat variable burst, which is frequently associated with a sleep spindle. Duration is greater than 0.5 s; amplitude is usually maximal at the frontal vertex. K complexes occur during non-REM sleep, apparently spontaneously or in response to sudden sensory or auditory stimuli, and are not specific for any individual sensory modality.

The appearance of the burst is somewhat variable, with the commonest form being a high-voltage negative slow wave followed by a smaller positive slow wave and frequent association with a sleep spindle. It exceeds 0.5 s in duration and usually has its maximum amplitude at the frontal vertex. K complexes are seen in non-REM sleep, apparently spontaneously or in response to sudden sensory or auditory stimuli, without specificity for one sensory modality.
Non-reactive sleep activity.
EEG activity consisting of normal sleep graphoelemts, but which cannot be interrupted by external stimuli/ the patient cannot be waken.

concept: Positive occipital sharp transient of sleep

concept: Positive occipital sharp transient of sleep

concept: Positive occipital sharp transient of sleep

concept: Positive occipital sharp transient of sleep

concept: Positive occipital sharp transient of sleep

Burst at 11-15 Hz but mostly at 12-14 Hz generally diffuse but of higher voltage over the central regions of the head, occurring during sleep. Amplitude varies but is mostly below 50 µV in the adult.
A sleep burst at 11-15 Hz, mostly 12-14 Hz, is generally diffuse but has higher voltage over central head regions. Amplitude varies, mostly remaining below 50 µV in adults.
During sleep, a generally diffuse burst occurs at 11-15 Hz, predominantly 12-14 Hz, with greater voltage centrally over the head. Its variable amplitude is mostly under 50 µV in the adult.
The burst appears in sleep at 11-15 Hz, most often 12-14 Hz, and is generally diffuse with higher voltage over central regions of the head. Adult amplitude varies but is mostly below 50 µV.
Generally diffuse sleep bursts have a frequency of 11-15 Hz, mainly 12-14 Hz, and greater voltage over central head regions. Their amplitude varies, mostly falling below 50 µV in adults.

A burst recorded during sleep is generally diffuse, with central head regions showing higher voltage, and occurs at 11-15 Hz, chiefly 12-14 Hz. In adults, amplitude is variable but mostly less than 50 µV.

At 11-15 Hz, predominantly 12-14 Hz, this burst occurs during sleep and is generally diffuse, though voltage is higher over central regions of the head. Amplitude in the adult varies and is mostly under 50 µV.
Higher voltage over central head regions characterizes an otherwise generally diffuse burst during sleep at 11-15 Hz, mostly 12-14 Hz. Its amplitude is variable but mostly below 50 µV in adults.
Vertex sharp transient

Sharp potential, maximal at the vertex, negative relative to other areas, apparently occurring spontaneously during sleep or in response to a sensory stimulus during sleep or wakefulness. May be single or repetitive. Amplitude varies but rarely exceeds 250 µV. Abbreviation: V wave. Synonym: vertex sharp wave.

A sharp potential is maximal at the vertex and negative relative to other areas, apparently occurring spontaneously in sleep or after a sensory stimulus during sleep or wakefulness. It may be single or repetitive; amplitude varies but rarely exceeds 250 µV. Its abbreviation is V wave and its synonym is vertex sharp wave.

The potential is sharp, greatest at the vertex, and negative compared with other areas. It apparently occurs spontaneously during sleep or in response to sensory stimulation in sleep or wakefulness, singly or repetitively. Amplitude varies and seldom exceeds 250 µV. V wave is the abbreviation; vertex sharp wave is the synonym.

Apparently spontaneous in sleep, or responsive to a sensory stimulus during sleep or wakefulness, this sharp potential has a vertex maximum and negativity relative to other areas. Single and repetitive occurrences are possible, with variable amplitude rarely above 250 µV. It is abbreviated V wave and also called vertex sharp wave.

A vertex-maximal sharp potential, negative relative to other areas, apparently appears spontaneously during sleep or after a sensory stimulus in sleep or wakefulness. It can occur singly or repeatedly, and its varying amplitude rarely exceeds 250 µV. The abbreviation is V wave; the synonymous term is vertex sharp wave.

This sharp potential reaches its maximum at the vertex and is negative relative to other areas; it apparently occurs spontaneously during sleep or follows sensory stimulation in sleep or wakefulness. It may be single or repetitive, with amplitude variable but rarely greater than 250 µV. V wave abbreviates it, and vertex sharp wave is a synonym.

Single or repetitive sharp potentials are maximal at the vertex and negative compared with other areas, apparently arising spontaneously in sleep or in response to a sensory stimulus during sleep or wakefulness. Amplitude varies, rarely exceeding 250 µV. The abbreviation V wave and synonym vertex sharp wave apply.

With variable amplitude rarely exceeding 250 µV, this sharp potential is greatest at the vertex and negative relative to other areas. It apparently occurs spontaneously during sleep or after a sensory stimulus during sleep or wakefulness, either singly or repetitively. Its abbreviation is V wave, and vertex sharp wave is its synonym.

Runs of rapid spikes

Bursts of spike discharges at a rate from 10 to 25/sec (in most cases somewhat irregular). The bursts last more than 2 seconds (usually 2 to 10 seconds) and it is typically seen in sleep. Synonyms: rhythmic spikes, generalized paroxysmal fast activity, fast paroxysmal rhythms, grand mal discharge, fast beta activity

Spike-discharge bursts occur at 10-25/sec, somewhat irregularly in most cases, and last more than 2 seconds, usually 2-10 seconds. They are typically seen during sleep. Synonyms are rhythmic spikes, generalized paroxysmal fast activity, fast paroxysmal rhythms, grand mal discharge, and fast beta activity.

Typically observed in sleep, these bursts contain spike discharges at 10-25/sec, most often somewhat irregular, and persist for over 2 seconds, usually 2-10 seconds. They are also termed rhythmic spikes, generalized paroxysmal fast activity, fast paroxysmal rhythms, grand mal discharge, or fast beta activity.

Bursts lasting longer than 2 seconds, usually 2-10 seconds, consist of spike discharges repeating at 10-25/sec, generally with some irregularity, and are typical in sleep. The synonymous terms are rhythmic spikes, generalized paroxysmal fast activity, fast paroxysmal rhythms, grand mal discharge, and fast beta activity.

At a rate of 10-25/sec, spike discharges form bursts that are somewhat irregular in most cases and last over 2 seconds, usually 2-10 seconds. Sleep is the typical setting. Equivalent terms include rhythmic spikes, generalized paroxysmal fast activity, fast paroxysmal rhythms, grand mal discharge, and fast beta activity.

The bursts are typically seen in sleep and have durations exceeding 2 seconds, generally 2-10 seconds. Their spike discharges occur at 10-25/sec and are somewhat irregular in most cases. Synonyms include rhythmic spikes, generalized paroxysmal fast activity, fast paroxysmal rhythms, grand mal discharge, and fast beta activity.

Spike discharges at 10-25/sec produce bursts, usually somewhat irregular, lasting more than 2 seconds and typically 2-10 seconds, seen characteristically in sleep. Rhythmic spikes, generalized paroxysmal fast activity, fast paroxysmal rhythms, grand mal discharge, and fast beta activity are synonymous expressions.

A burst comprises spike discharges at a usually somewhat irregular rate of 10-25/sec. Duration exceeds 2 seconds, commonly 2-10 seconds, and occurrence is typical during sleep. These bursts are also called rhythmic spikes, generalized paroxysmal fast activity, fast paroxysmal rhythms, grand mal discharge, and fast beta activity.
Sharp wave

A transient clearly distinguished from background activity, with pointed peak at a conventional paper speed or time scale, and duration of 70-200 ms, i.e. over ¼-1/5 s approximately. Main component is generally negative relative to other areas. Amplitude varies. Comments: 1. Term should be restricted to epileptiform discharges and does not apply to (a) distinctive physiologic events such as vertex sharp transients, lambda waves, and positive occipital sharp transients of sleep, (b) sharp transients poorly distinguished from background activity and sharp-appearing individual waves of EEG rhythms. 2. Sharp waves should be differentiated from spikes, i.e. transients having similar characteristics but shorter duration. However, it should be kept in mind that this distinction is largely arbitrary and primarily serves descriptive purposes.

A transient is clearly distinct from background activity, has a pointed peak at conventional paper speed or time scale, and lasts 70-200 ms, approximately over ¼-1/5 s. Its main component is generally negative relative to other areas, and amplitude varies. The term is restricted to epileptiform discharges and excludes distinctive physiologic events such as vertex sharp transients, lambda waves, and positive occipital sharp transients of sleep, as well as sharp transients poorly distinguished from background activity and sharp-appearing individual waves of EEG rhythms. Sharp waves should be distinguished from spikes, which share similar characteristics but are shorter; this distinction is largely arbitrary and mainly descriptive.

Clearly distinguishable from background activity, this transient has a pointed peak on a conventional paper speed or time scale and a duration of 70-200 ms, approximately over ¼-1/5 s. Amplitude is variable, while the main component is usually negative compared with other areas. Use the term only for epileptiform discharges, not for distinctive physiologic events including vertex sharp transients, lambda waves, and positive occipital sharp transients of sleep, or for poorly background-differentiated sharp transients and sharp-looking individual waves of EEG rhythms. Differentiate sharp waves from spikes, transients of similar characteristics but shorter duration, while recognizing that the distinction is largely arbitrary and primarily descriptive.

At conventional paper speed or time scale, the transient has a pointed peak and is clearly separated from background activity; it lasts 70-200 ms, approximately over ¼-1/5 s. The amplitude varies and the principal component is generally negative relative to other areas. The expression should apply only to epileptiform discharges, excluding distinctive physiologic events such as vertex sharp transients, lambda waves, and positive occipital sharp transients of sleep, sharp transients not well distinguished from background activity, and sharp-appearing individual EEG rhythm waves. Spikes have similar characteristics with shorter duration and should be differentiated from sharp waves, although the distinction is largely arbitrary and chiefly serves description.

A duration of 70-200 ms, approximately over ¼-1/5 s, characterizes a transient clearly differentiated from background activity with a pointed peak at conventional paper speed or time scale. The main component usually has negative polarity relative to other areas; its amplitude is variable. Restrict this term to epileptiform discharges: it does not cover distinctive physiologic events such as vertex sharp transients, lambda waves, and positive occipital sharp transients of sleep, nor sharp transients poorly separated from the background or individual EEG rhythm waves with a sharp appearance. Sharp waves require differentiation from shorter-duration transients with similar characteristics, namely spikes; the distinction remains largely arbitrary and serves mainly descriptive purposes.

The transient, clearly distinguished from the background, peaks sharply at conventional paper speed or time scale and lasts 70-200 ms, approximately over ¼-1/5 s. There is variation in amplitude, and the main component is generally negative compared with other areas. Only epileptiform discharges should receive this term; distinctive physiologic events, for example vertex sharp transients, lambda waves, and positive occipital sharp transients of sleep, are excluded, as are poorly background-differentiated sharp transients and sharp-appearing individual EEG rhythm waves. Distinguish sharp waves from spikes of similar characteristics but shorter duration, bearing in mind that this largely arbitrary distinction primarily serves descriptive purposes.

This transient stands clearly apart from background activity and shows a pointed peak at conventional paper speed or time scale, with duration 70-200 ms, approximately over ¼-1/5 s. Generally negative relative to other areas, its main component has variable amplitude. The term should be limited to epileptiform discharges rather than distinctive physiologic events such as vertex sharp transients, lambda waves, and positive occipital sharp transients of sleep, or sharp transients poorly distinguished from background activity and sharp-looking individual waves of EEG rhythms. Compared with sharp waves, spikes are shorter transients with otherwise similar characteristics; they should be differentiated, though the distinction is mostly arbitrary and primarily descriptive.

A clearly distinguishable transient differs from background activity, has a pointed peak at conventional paper speed or time scale, and persists for 70-200 ms, approximately over ¼-1/5 s. Amplitude varies; relative to other areas, the main component is generally negative. Apply the term exclusively to epileptiform discharges, excluding distinctive physiologic events like vertex sharp transients, lambda waves, and positive occipital sharp transients of sleep, together with sharp transients poorly distinguished from background activity and sharp-appearing individual waves of EEG rhythms. The differentiation of sharp waves from spikes, similar transients of shorter duration, should be maintained, recognizing its largely arbitrary and primarily descriptive nature.

A sequence of a sharp wave and a slow wave.
A sharp wave is followed in sequence by a slow wave.
The sequence comprises a sharp wave and then a slow wave.
A slow wave follows a sharp wave in this sequence.

Slow sharp wave
A transient that bears all the characteristics of a sharp-wave, but exceeds 200 ms. Synonym: blunted sharp wave.
A transient has every characteristic of a sharp wave but lasts longer than 200 ms; blunted sharp wave is a synonym.
This transient resembles a sharp wave in all characteristics, except that its duration exceeds 200 ms. It is also called a blunted sharp wave.
With a duration greater than 200 ms, the transient otherwise has all sharp-wave characteristics and is synonymous with blunted sharp wave.
All the characteristics of a sharp wave are present in a transient lasting over 200 ms, also termed a blunted sharp wave.
The transient is a sharp wave in all characteristics but exceeds 200 ms in duration; its synonym is blunted sharp wave.
Blunted sharp wave is the synonymous term for a transient with all sharp-wave characteristics but a duration longer than 200 ms.
A transient lasting more than 200 ms retains all characteristics of a sharp wave and is also known as a blunted sharp wave.
Spike

A transient, clearly distinguished from background activity, with pointed peak at a conventional paper speed or time scale and duration from 20 to under 70 ms, i.e. 1/50-1/15 s approximately. Main component is generally negative relative to other areas. Amplitude varies. Comments: 1. Term should be restricted to epileptiform discharges. EEG spikes should be differentiated from sharp waves, i.e. transients having similar characteristics but longer duration. However, it should be kept in mind that this distinction is largely arbitrary and primarily serves descriptive purposes. 2. A slow negative component may trail the spike discharge and often attain the same amplitude as the negative main component of the spike. This trailing component of a single spike should not be regarded as evidence of a spike-and-slow-wave complex.

A transient clearly distinct from background activity has a pointed peak at conventional paper speed or time scale and lasts 20 to under 70 ms, approximately 1/50-1/15 s. Amplitude varies, and the main component is generally negative relative to other areas. Restrict the term to epileptiform discharges and distinguish EEG spikes from sharp waves, which have similar characteristics but longer duration. The distinction is largely arbitrary and primarily descriptive. A slow negative component may follow the spike discharge and often reaches the amplitude of the spike's negative main component; this trailing component of a single spike is not evidence of a spike-and-slow-wave complex.

The transient is clearly distinguishable from background activity, peaks pointedly at conventional paper speed or time scale, and has duration from 20 to less than 70 ms, approximately 1/50-1/15 s. The principal component is usually negative compared with other areas, with variable amplitude. Use this term only for epileptiform discharges. EEG spikes should be differentiated from longer-duration sharp waves of similar characteristics, recognizing that the distinction is largely arbitrary and chiefly descriptive. The spike discharge may be followed by a slow negative component, often as large as its negative main component. Such a trailing component of one spike should not be taken as evidence of a spike-and-slow-wave complex.

At conventional paper speed or time scale, this transient has a pointed peak and stands clearly apart from background activity; its duration is 20 to under 70 ms, about 1/50-1/15 s. Its amplitude is variable; the main component is generally negative relative to other areas. The term should be confined to epileptiform discharges; EEG spikes differ from sharp waves of similar characteristics by their shorter duration, although this distinction is largely arbitrary and mainly descriptive. A slow negative component can trail a spike discharge, frequently attaining the same amplitude as the negative main component, but that trailing component of a single spike should not be regarded as evidence for a spike-and-slow-wave complex.

Lasting from 20 to below 70 ms, approximately 1/50-1/15 s, the transient is clearly differentiated from background activity and has a pointed peak at conventional paper speed or time scale. The main component generally has negative polarity relative to other areas, and amplitude varies. Only epileptiform discharges should receive the term. Differentiate EEG spikes from sharp waves, which are similar but longer, while keeping in mind the largely arbitrary and primarily descriptive nature of the distinction. Following the spike discharge, there may be a slow negative component often matching the amplitude of the spike's negative main component. This component following a single spike does not constitute evidence of a spike-and-slow-wave complex.

A clearly background-differentiated transient shows a pointed peak at conventional paper speed or time scale, with duration 20 to under 70 ms, approximately 1/50-1/15 s. Compared with other areas, the main component is generally negative; the amplitude varies. Limit the expression to epileptiform discharges and differentiate EEG spikes from otherwise similar sharp waves of longer duration; this differentiation is largely arbitrary and serves principally descriptive purposes. A trailing slow negative component may occur after the spike discharge and often equal its negative main component in amplitude; for a single spike, this trailing component should not be considered evidence of a spike-and-slow-wave complex.

The transient lasts 20 to less than 70 ms, approximately 1/50-1/15 s, is clearly distinct from the background, and has a pointed peak at conventional paper speed or time scale. Variable amplitude accompanies a main component generally negative relative to other areas. The term applies only to epileptiform discharges. Sharp waves are longer transients of similar characteristics and should be distinguished from EEG spikes, though the distinction is largely arbitrary and primarily serves description. The discharge may have a subsequent slow negative component, often reaching the same amplitude as the spike's main negative component. A single spike's trailing component should not be interpreted as evidence of a spike-and-slow-wave complex.

A pointed peak on a conventional paper speed or time scale characterizes a transient clearly distinguished from background activity, with duration from 20 to under 70 ms, approximately 1/50-1/15 s. There is amplitude variation, while the main component is usually negative in relation to other areas. EEG spikes should be differentiated from sharp waves with similar characteristics but greater duration, bearing in mind that this largely arbitrary distinction is primarily descriptive. The term should be restricted to epileptiform discharges. A slow negative component may follow the spike discharge and often has the same amplitude as the negative main component of the spike. Its presence after a single spike should not be treated as evidence of a spike-and-slow-wave complex.

A pattern consisting of a spike followed by a slow wave
The pattern comprises a spike followed by a slow wave.
A spike and a subsequent slow wave make up the pattern.
A slow wave follows a spike in this pattern.
The pattern is formed by a spike preceding a slow wave.
This is a pattern in which a spike is followed by a slow wave.
The pattern begins with a spike and continues with a slow wave.
A spike followed in sequence by a slow wave constitutes the pattern.
Spike-and-slow-wave runs: Classical 3/s ~

Characteristic paroxysm consisting of a regular sequence of spike-and-slow-wave complexes which: (1) repeat at 3-3.5 c/s (measured during the first few seconds of the paroxysm), (2) are bilateral in their onset and termination, generalized, and usually of the maximum amplitude over the frontal areas, (3) are approximately synchronous and symmetrical on the two sides of the head throughout the paroxysm.

A characteristic paroxysm comprises a regular sequence of spike-and-slow-wave complexes at 3-3.5 c/s, measured in its first few seconds. Onset and termination are bilateral; the complexes are generalized and usually largest over frontal areas, remaining approximately synchronous and symmetrical across both sides of the head throughout the paroxysm.

The paroxysm characteristically consists of regularly sequenced spike-and-slow-wave complexes repeating at 3-3.5 c/s during measurement in the first few seconds. They begin and end bilaterally, are generalized with usually maximal frontal amplitude, and are approximately synchronous and symmetrical on the two head sides throughout.

Spike-and-slow-wave complexes form a regular sequence in this characteristic paroxysm. Their rate is 3-3.5 c/s when measured in the first few seconds, their onset and termination are bilateral, and they are generalized, usually maximal in frontal amplitude. Approximate synchrony and symmetry between both head sides persist throughout the paroxysm.

Throughout the characteristic paroxysm, spike-and-slow-wave complexes are approximately synchronous and symmetrical on both head sides. They form a regular sequence at 3-3.5 c/s, measured during the first few seconds, are bilateral at onset and termination, and are generalized with usually greatest amplitude over frontal areas.

This characteristic paroxysm features a regular succession of generalized spike-and-slow-wave complexes, usually maximal frontally, with bilateral onset and termination. They repeat at 3-3.5 c/s as measured in the first few seconds and remain approximately synchronous and symmetrical across the two sides of the head throughout.

A regular train of spike-and-slow-wave complexes characterizes the paroxysm, with a frequency of 3-3.5 c/s measured during its first few seconds. Bilateral onset and termination accompany generalized distribution and usually maximal frontal amplitude; the complexes are approximately synchronous and symmetrical on both head sides throughout the paroxysm.

The characteristic paroxysm consists of spike-and-slow-wave complexes in regular sequence, repeating at 3-3.5 c/s in measurements during its first few seconds. Generalized complexes usually reach maximum amplitude frontally, begin and end bilaterally, and maintain approximate synchrony and symmetry on the two sides of the head for the entire paroxysm.
Spike-and-slow-wave runs: Slow 1-2.5/s ~

Spike-and-slow-wave complexes which consist of a rather slow spike (according to definition, a sharp wave, lasting 70 msec or longer and a slow wave), repeat at 1-2.5 Hz frequency, and are bilateral synchronous (generalized) with a frontal midline maximum.

Spike-and-slow-wave complexes contain a rather slow spike, defined as a sharp wave lasting at least 70 msec, and a slow wave. They repeat at 1-2.5 Hz, are bilaterally synchronous (generalized), and have a frontal midline maximum.

A rather slow spike, by definition a sharp wave of 70 msec or longer, and a slow wave compose complexes recurring at 1-2.5 Hz. These spike-and-slow-wave complexes are bilateral and synchronous (generalized), with maximum over the frontal midline.

At 1-2.5 Hz, bilaterally synchronous (generalized) spike-and-slow-wave complexes reach a frontal midline maximum. Each consists of a rather slow spike, which by definition is a sharp wave lasting 70 msec or more, together with a slow wave.

The complexes comprise a rather slow spike, corresponding by definition to a sharp wave of at least 70 msec, plus a slow wave. Their spike-and-slow-wave repetition rate is 1-2.5 Hz, their distribution bilateral synchronous (generalized), and their maximum at the frontal midline.

These generalized, bilaterally synchronous spike-and-slow-wave complexes recur at 1-2.5 Hz and are maximal at the frontal midline. A rather slow spike, defined as a sharp wave lasting 70 msec or longer, is combined with a slow wave.

A sharp wave lasting at least 70 msec constitutes the rather slow spike by definition in these spike-and-slow-wave complexes, alongside a slow wave. Repetition occurs at 1-2.5 Hz, bilaterally and synchronously (generalized), with a frontal midline maximum.

With a frontal midline maximum, the spike-and-slow-wave complexes are bilateral synchronous (generalized) and repeat at 1-2.5 Hz. Their components are a rather slow spike, by definition a sharp wave of 70 msec or longer, and a slow wave.

Spike-and-slow-wave complexes which repeat at 4 or 4-5/s, are bilateral, usually of the maximum amplitude over the frontal areas, are approximately synchronous and symmetrical on the two sides of the head throughout the paroxysm.
Spike-and-slow-wave complexes recur at 4 or 4-5/s, are bilateral and usually largest frontally, and remain approximately synchronous and symmetrical on both head sides throughout the paroxysm.

Throughout the paroxysm, bilateral spike-and-slow-wave complexes repeat at 4 or 4-5/s with approximate synchrony and symmetry between the two head sides, usually reaching maximum amplitude over frontal areas.

The complexes repeat at 4 or 4-5/s bilaterally, generally with highest amplitude frontally. These spike-and-slow-wave complexes are approximately synchronous and symmetrical across both sides of the head for the duration of the paroxysm.

A repetition rate of 4 or 4-5/s characterizes bilateral spike-and-slow-wave complexes that are usually maximal over frontal areas and approximately synchronous and symmetrical on both head sides throughout the paroxysm.
Bilateral spike-and-slow-wave complexes, usually largest in frontal areas, recur at 4 or 4-5/s and preserve approximate synchrony and symmetry between both sides of the head throughout the paroxysm.

The spike-and-slow-wave complexes are bilateral, repeat at 4 or 4-5/s, and usually have their greatest amplitude over frontal areas; they remain approximately synchronous and symmetrical on the two sides of the head throughout the paroxysm.

Approximate synchrony and symmetry on both head sides persist throughout the paroxysm for these bilateral spike-and-slow-wave complexes, which repeat at 4 or 4-5/s and are usually maximal in amplitude frontally.

Paroxysms consisting of an irregular sequence of spike-and-slow-wave complexes, that occur bilaterally but do not meet the criteria of the above described subtypes.
Paroxysms comprise an irregular sequence of bilateral spike-and-slow-wave complexes that do not meet the criteria for the subtypes described above.

In these paroxysms, an irregular sequence of spike-and-slow-wave complexes occurs on both sides but does not meet the criteria for the subtypes described above.
Delta activity
Rhythm with frequency of under 4 Hz; clearly exceeds the amount considered physiologically normal for the patient’s age and state of alertness.

The rhythm has a frequency under 4 Hz and clearly exceeds the amount considered physiologically normal for the patient's age and state of alertness.

A frequency below 4 Hz characterizes a rhythm whose amount clearly exceeds physiologic normality for the patient's age and level of alertness.

Thy represent the EEG feature of a severe ongoing central nervus system disease with certain paroxysmal or even overt epileptogenic properties.

Triphasic waves

High amplitude (over 70 µV) positive sharp transients, which are preceded and followed by relatively low amplitude negative waves. The first negative wave generally has a lower amplitude than the negative afterwave. The distribution is generalized, and frequently the largest deflections in a bipolar fronto- occipital derivation occur at the frontal electrodes. Triphasic waves tend to have a repetition rate of ca. 1- 2 Hz.

High-amplitude positive sharp transients over 70 µV are preceded and followed by relatively low-amplitude negative waves, the first generally smaller than the negative afterwave. Distribution is generalized; in a bipolar fronto-occipital derivation, the largest deflections are frequently at frontal electrodes. Triphasic waves tend to repeat at about 1-2 Hz.

Positive sharp transients exceeding 70 µV have relatively low-amplitude negative waves before and after them, with the initial negative wave usually smaller than the afterwave. They are generalized, and bipolar fronto-occipital derivations frequently show the greatest deflections at frontal electrodes. The repetition rate of triphasic waves tends to be approximately 1-2 Hz.

The distribution is generalized, with the largest deflections frequently at frontal electrodes in bipolar fronto-occipital derivations. Absence: - Atypical

Absence seizures may have a) change in tone that are more pronounced than in typical absences; b) onset and /or cessation that is not abrupt. Ictal EEG: it is more heterogeneous; may include irregular spike-and- slow wave complexes, fast activity or other paroxysmal activity. Abnormalities are bilateral but often irregular and asymmetrical. Interictal EEG: background is usually abnormal; paroxysmal activity (such as spikes and spike-and-slow wave complexes) frequently irregular and asymmetrical.

Absence: - Typical

Clinical manifestations can be: a) impairment of consciousness only; b) with mild clonic components; c) with atonic components; d) with tonic components; e) with automatisms; f) with autonomic components (b through f may be used alone or in combination). Interictal EEG: background activity usually normal although paroxysmal activity (such as spikes or spike-and-slow-wave complexes) may occur. This activity is usually regular and symmetrical.

Clinical manifestations may consist of impaired consciousness alone or include mild clonic, atonic, tonic, autonomic components, or automatisms, each alone or combined. Interictal background is usually normal, but paroxysmal activity such as spikes or spike-and-slow-wave complexes may occur and is usually regular and symmetrical.

Eyelid myoclonia - with (or without) absence

Episodes characterized by occurrence of eyelid myoclonia, i.e. marked jerking of the eyelids immediately after eye closure with or without brief absences, usually lasting less than 6 sec. Ictal EEG: high-amplitude generalized polyspikes or polyspikewave complexes, often followed by brief discharges (3–6 s or less) of rhythmic spike- or polyspike-wave complexes at 3 or more per second. Typically, these abnormalities are triggered by active eye-closure (not by simple eye blinks), occurring immediately (usually about 0.5s) on closing the eyes, in a well-lit recording room; darkness abolishes totally or partially this response, whereas hyperventilation can enhance generalized paroxysmal activity and eventually give rise to eyelids myoclonia and absences. Interictal EEG: generalized photoparoxysmal EEG response

Myoclonic absence

Absence seizure characterized by abrupt onset associated with bilateral rhythmic myoclonic jerks of severe intensity. The loss of consciousness during the absence may be complete or partial. The seizure mainly involves muscles of the shoulders, arms, and legs; facial muscles are less involved. When facial myoclonias occur, they are more evident around the chin and mouth, whereas eyelid twitching is typically absent or rare. The movements may be sustained and progressive, being associated with tonic contraction, which is maximal in shoulder and deltoid muscles. The jerks and tonic contractions may be symmetrical or predominant on one side, causing turning of the head and body. Autonomic manifestations such as arrest of respiratory movement and urinary incontinence may also be present. Each episode of myoclonic absences may last from 10 to 60 seconds. Ictal EEG in epilepsy with myoclonic absences shows a pattern of bilateral, synchronous, and symmetrical discharge of spike-waves at 3 Hz, similar to that of childhood absences. The discharges may end with delta waves in frontal areas, which may be asymmetrical. The spike-wave discharges may be interspersed with polyspike and wave activity. Polygraphic recording of myoclonic absences discloses the appearance of bilateral myoclonias, at the same frequency as the spikes and waves, which begin 1 or 2 seconds after the onset of the EEG paroxysmal discharges and are followed by a tonic, sometimes asymmetrical, contraction, maximal in the deltoid and shoulder muscles. Interictal EEG findings include normal background activity in all cases with superimposed generalized spikes and waves or, more rarely, focal or multifocal spikes and waves. Photosensitivity is uncommon. The sleep EEG shows a normal organization and symmetrical physiological patterns. During sleep the evolution of the spikes and waves is similar, on the whole, to that observed in childhood absence epilepsy

concept: Subclinical rhythmic EEG discharge of adults
text: A rhythmic pattern seen in the adult age group, mainly in the waking state or drowsiness. It consists of a mixture of frequencies, often predominant in the theta range. The onset may be fairly abrupt with widespread sharp rhythmical theta and occasionally with delta activity.
